question: What does df.repartition(n) do?
options: Reduces partitions without a shuffle by merging adjacent partitions
Performs a full shuffle to redistribute data into exactly n partitions
Sorts the DataFrame globally across n files
Caches the DataFrame into n memory blocks
explanation: repartition triggers a full shuffle to redistribute rows evenly (round-robin, or hashed when columns are given) into n partitions. It can both increase or decrease partition count, unlike coalesce which only reduces.

question: When is repartition preferred over coalesce?
options: When you want to reduce partitions cheaply without moving data
When you want to avoid any shuffle at all costs
When writing a single output file
When you need to increase partitions or produce evenly balanced partitions
explanation: repartition is the right choice when increasing partition count or when you need well-balanced partitions, because it does a full shuffle. coalesce cannot increase partitions and may leave data skewed since it only merges existing partitions.

question: What does df.repartition("country") accomplish?
options: It sorts rows by country within each existing partition
It creates exactly one partition per distinct country guaranteed
It hash-partitions rows so all rows with the same country land in the same partition
It filters the DataFrame to only distinct countries
explanation: Column-based repartition hash-partitions the data on the given key, so all rows sharing a country value are colocated in the same partition. The number of partitions defaults to spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, not necessarily one per distinct value.

question: Repartitioning on a key before a join on that key can help because it:
options: Can reduce or avoid an additional shuffle during the join by pre-colocating matching keys
Guarantees a broadcast join will be used
Eliminates the need to read the data from source
Converts the join into a narrow transformation with no data movement ever
explanation: Pre-partitioning both sides on the join key colocates matching rows, which can let the join proceed without an extra shuffle. It does not make the join narrow in general, and it does not force a broadcast join.

question: A common performance pitfall with repartition is:
options: It never causes a shuffle, so it is always free
It permanently deletes rows that don't fit in the new partitions
It can only be called once per SparkSession
The full shuffle it triggers is expensive, so unnecessary repartitions waste network and I/O
explanation: Because repartition always performs a full shuffle, calling it needlessly adds significant network transfer, serialization, and disk I/O cost. It should be used deliberately, for example to fix skew or set output parallelism, not sprinkled everywhere.
